findings.title: No rate limiting on share creation endpoint
findings.description: The POST /api/new endpoint has no rate limiting or abuse prevention. An attacker can flood the Durable Object storage with arbitrary snippets, potentially causing denial of service and increased Cloudflare billing costs. There is no CAPTCHA, API key requirement, or IP-based throttling.
findings.recommendation: Implement rate limiting using Cloudflare's built-in rate limiting rules, or add per-IP throttling logic in the Worker. Consider adding a CAPTCHA for the browser form submission.

findings.title: No CORS restrictions on API endpoints
findings.description: The API endpoints /api/new and /api/delete do not set any CORS headers or validate the Origin header. While this means browsers will block cross-origin reads by default, the lack of explicit CORS policy means the endpoints can be called from any origin without preflight checks (simple POST with application/json would require preflight, but the server does not reject cross-origin requests server-side). A malicious page could potentially trigger state-changing operations.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit CORS headers restricting allowed origins to the deployed domain. Validate the Origin header on state-changing requests. Consider adding CSRF tokens for form submissions.

findings.title: No CSRF protection on state-changing POST endpoints
findings.description: The /api/new and /api/delete endpoints accept POST requests with JSON bodies but do not validate any CSRF token, Origin header, or Referer header. While the Content-Type: application/json requirement provides some implicit protection (browsers require preflight for non-simple content types in cross-origin requests), the server does not enforce or verify the Content-Type, so an attacker could craft a form submission.
findings.recommendation: Validate the Origin or Referer header on POST requests to ensure they match the expected domain. Consider implementing CSRF tokens.

findings.title: Delete token stored in browser localStorage without encryption
findings.description: The deleteToken (which authorizes snippet deletion) is stored in plaintext in the browser's localStorage under the key 'keyshare-items'. Any XSS vulnerability (even from browser extensions or other scripts on the same origin) could exfiltrate all delete tokens. localStorage is also accessible to any JavaScript running on the same origin.
findings.recommendation: Consider using HttpOnly cookies for delete authorization instead of localStorage-based tokens. If localStorage must be used, document the risk clearly. The current design is acceptable for a low-sensitivity text-sharing tool but limits the security ceiling.

findings.title: Timing-based side channel in delete token comparison
findings.description: The delete token comparison in the KeyshareStore /delete handler uses strict equality (row.delete_token !== deleteToken), which is a non-constant-time string comparison. This could theoretically leak information about the delete token through timing differences, although exploitation is extremely difficult over a network and with UUID-length tokens.
findings.recommendation: Use a constant-time comparison function (e.g., crypto.subtle.timingSafeEqual or a manual implementation) for comparing secret tokens. The practical risk is very low given the token length and network latency, but it is a defense-in-depth best practice.

findings.title: Single Durable Object instance is a bottleneck and single point of failure
findings.description: All snippets are stored in a single Durable Object instance identified by the name 'primary' (env.STORE.idFromName('primary')). This creates a single point of failure and a scalability bottleneck. A targeted attack could overwhelm this single instance, and all data resides in one location.
findings.recommendation: Consider sharding data across multiple Durable Object instances (e.g., by hashing the snippet ID) to improve resilience and scalability. For a small-scale tool this is acceptable, but be aware of the limitation.

findings.title: No Content-Security-Policy header on HTML pages
findings.description: The HTML responses do not include a Content-Security-Policy (CSP) header. While the application uses inline scripts and styles (which would require 'unsafe-inline'), a properly configured CSP could still restrict external resource loading. Currently, external fonts are loaded from fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com. Without CSP, if an XSS vector were found, there would be no browser-level mitigation.
findings.recommendation: Add a Content-Security-Policy header. At minimum, restrict script-src and style-src. Consider using nonces for inline scripts/styles. Add other security headers: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Referrer-Policy.

findings.title: No authentication or access control for viewing shared content
findings.description: Anyone with the share URL (/s/:id) can view the shared content. The UUID-based ID provides unguessability (128-bit random via crypto.randomUUID()), but there is no additional authentication such as a password or access token. This is by design for a simple sharing tool, but users should understand that the URL is the only secret protecting the content.
findings.recommendation: Document clearly that the URL is the sole access control mechanism. Consider adding an optional password/PIN feature for sensitive content. The current design using crypto.randomUUID() provides adequate unguessability for most use cases.

findings.title: Shared content is stored in plaintext (no encryption at rest)
findings.description: Snippet text is stored as plaintext in the Durable Object SQLite database. Anyone with access to the Cloudflare account or Durable Object storage can read all stored snippets. For a 'keyshare' tool that may be used to share sensitive credentials, this is a notable concern.
findings.recommendation: Consider implementing client-side encryption (e.g., using the Web Crypto API) so that the server only stores ciphertext. The decryption key could be included in the URL fragment (which is not sent to the server). This would provide true end-to-end encryption for shared secrets.

findings.title: No package.json or dependency lockfile in repository
findings.description: The repository contains only wrangler.toml and src/index.ts with no package.json, package-lock.json, or other dependency manifest. While this means there are no third-party npm dependencies to audit (a positive), it also means the build/deploy process is not documented and may rely on globally installed tools with unknown versions.
findings.recommendation: Add a package.json with the wrangler dependency pinned to a specific version, and commit a lockfile. This ensures reproducible builds and allows dependency vulnerability scanning.

findings.title: XSS in error page title and message parameters (internal only)
findings.description: The renderErrorPage function interpolates its title and message parameters directly into HTML without escaping. However, these parameters are only called with hardcoded string literals within the codebase, so this is not currently exploitable. If future code passes user-controlled data to renderErrorPage, it would become an XSS vulnerability.
findings.recommendation: Apply escapeHtml() to the title and message parameters in renderErrorPage as a defense-in-depth measure, even though current callers only pass hardcoded strings.

findings.title: No logging or audit trail for security-relevant operations
findings.description: The application does not log creation, access, or deletion of snippets. There is no way to detect or investigate abuse, brute-force attempts on delete tokens, or unauthorized access patterns.
findings.recommendation: Add structured logging for security-relevant events (creation, access, deletion, failed deletion attempts) including timestamps and client IP addresses. Cloudflare Workers provides console.log which integrates with Logpush.

findings.title: No request size limit on POST endpoints
findings.description: The /api/new and /api/delete endpoints call request.json() without first checking Content-Length or enforcing a body size limit. While the text field is validated to TEXT_LIMIT (10000 chars) after parsing, an attacker could send a very large JSON payload (e.g., deeply nested or with huge extraneous fields) to consume Worker CPU and memory during JSON parsing.
findings.recommendation: Check the Content-Length header before parsing and reject requests exceeding a reasonable limit (e.g., 16KB). Cloudflare Workers has a default body size limit, but explicit validation provides defense-in-depth.
